newsitem.title: USA: U.S. leadership in IMF, World Bank at risk - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: U.S. leadership in IMF, World Bank at risk - Rubin.

text.p: U.S. leadership in such international organizations as the IMF and World Bank will be put at risk if America does not provide them with the money it has promised, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Thursday.
"This year is critical," he said in remarks prepared for delivery to a House Appropriations subcommittee. "If we do not meet our commitments, we will jeopardize our leadership in these institutions."
The United States is behind on its payments to the international financial institutions to the tune of over $1.5 billion, Rubin said.
The Clinton administration is seeking Congressional approval of $1.6 billion for the institutions in the year starting on Oct. 1, including about $300 million to partially pay down those arrears.
Rubin warned that failure to meet U.S. commitments would hurt America's foreign policy interests in such diverse area as Bosnia, the former Soviet Union and the Middle East.
"We cannot lead with other people's money," he said.
Rubin said that the international organizations have already made great progress in getting a better grip on their costs and making their operations more open.
The World Bank last week unveiled a major reform plan designed to give new muscle to its front-line development operations at a two-year cost of as much as $570 million.
Rubin said the proposed reform plan responds even more than before to past criticisms of the Bank. "But it also has a significant price tag," he said, "and we are carefully reviewing its details."

The administration is also seeking $3.5 billion in budget authority for U.S. participation in the International Monetary Fund's New Arrangements to Borrow -- a war chest for use in financial emergencies.
"This request is critical to supporting the IMF's primary role of promoting international monetary stability by preventing financial shocks and responding to crises that may emerge," Rubin said.

He added that the United States and the rest of the IMF's member nations are also discussing a possible increase in the Fund's normal financial reources, or quotas, and pledged to continue to consult with Congress about that.
